PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #1: Recognize opinion topics — Grade 2

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that writers share stories (narratives) and teach information (via informatives) to their readers. But writers can also share their feelings, beliefs, and opinions. Today, I'm going to teach you how to tell if you're reading an opinion — or not.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing starts with an opinion. An opinion tells what the writer thinks, feels, or believes about a topic that has different sides or choices. Unlike facts — which are right or wrong — opinions are neither. They are simply different. Two people can read about the same topic and believe completely different things. (Introduce the icons & hand gestures.)

When a reader recognizes that a piece of writing is persuasive, he understands: the writer is going to share what HE thinks and explain why his choice is best.

WHY the skill is important | If a reader cannot tell the difference between opinions and facts, he may confuse what the writer believes with fact. Persuasive writing has a different purpose than informative writing. When readers recognize persuasive writing, they understand: "This is what the author believes." Then they can read and decide whether or not to agree.

HOW the skill works | After reading a little bit of the text…
1. ASK: Is the author describing what happened to characters? If yes, then it's a narrative story.
2. ASK: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? If yes, then it's informative writing.
3. ASK: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings on a topic? Look for opinion words like "I think, favorite, the best." Ask yourself: Could someone have a different opinion on this same topic? If yes, then it's persuasive writing.

This is how readers determine if a writer is revealing a story, telling facts, or sharing his opinion.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I figure out what type of writing this is. Project Lunch Text A and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a main character. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to individual sentences.) "School lunches offer a variety of food and drink choices." That's a fact. "These foods help give students energy for the rest of the day." Everyone agrees with that. "Choosing a balanced meal helps the body stay healthy." Yep — that's true information, too. Everything here sounds like facts everyone agrees on. But let me check the third writing purpose before I decide.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings about a topic? Let me look for opinion words like — I think, My favorite, always, the best. (Scan slowly, pointing.) I don't see any. And he's not taking a side. This is NOT persuasive.
So it's definitely not a story or an opinion. This text includes facts everyone agrees on. This is informative writing.

OK, I'm going to do this again. I'm going to determine if the author is sharing an opinion with me/the reader. Project Lunch Text B and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a character or a problem. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to the first sentence.) "Smoothies can include fruits like strawberries, bananas, and blueberries." That sounds like a fact. "These drinks provide important vitamins." That's probably true too. (Pause.) But wait — "Adding fresh fruit smoothies to the lunch menu would give students a healthy and refreshing option." Would everyone agree with that? Does every school need smoothies on the menu? That doesn't feel like something everyone agrees on. Let me think through the persuasive lens.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings about a topic? (Point to the first sentence again. Point/Reread the last sentence, too.) "Fresh fruit smoothies would be a smart addition to the lunch menu." Smart — I'm questioning if that's an opinion word? It's not "I think" or "I believe" — but "smart addition" is describing what the author thinks about this idea. Someone else might think water or milk is a better drink choice. So the author is trying to convince the reader to agree. This is persuasive writing.

Today, we are learning how to recognize the signals that reveal if an author is sharing his opinion — if he is writing persuasively.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example. Project Recess Game Text A. Read it aloud quickly. Do not ask students to comment.

Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say no — there's no character and nothing is happening to anyone. Let's keep going.

2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? Point to "The game involves running, quick thinking, and teamwork." Is that true for everyone who plays tag? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say yes — that does sound like a fact about tag. Let's look at one more sentence before we decide. Point to "Tag is a great choice for a fun and active recess game." Do you see any opinion words in that sentence? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say "great." Does everyone agree that tag is the greatest recess game? Could someone think a different game is better? (Nod.) Hmm… so what type of writing is this? 1… 2… 3… Blurt! Persuasive — right!

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to tell when a writer is sharing his opinion — or not. If we can recognize opinions, then we are closer to being able to write them.

During Independent Writing Time, your job is to read several short texts and apply the same process. You will mark the text with a "P" if you determine it's persuasive and shares an opinion. Mark an "I" if it's informative and teaches facts. Mark an "E" if it's an entertaining narrative story. Let's go be writers!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (1 of 2) — Grade 2

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that persuasive writing is about choices — it's about picking a side and writing about what you think. But how do you pick which side to write about? Today, I'm going to teach you how to determine which side is the strongest.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing is more than just your opinion — it's the strongest opinion that you can prove. Writers don't "pick" a side right away. First they think carefully about both choices.

WHY the skill is important | The strongest side is the one you can say the most about. If you pick a side too fast, you might miss a stronger one. Thinking through both sides first helps you find the one with the most to say.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Look at your topic. What are the two choices? Don't pick yet — just name them.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. It's hard not to blurt out your favorite right away. (Demonstrate hand over your mouth.) We slow down and think first.

Step 3: Think like one side. (Reveal the blue hat.) Writers put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best — even if your heart isn't there. (Teach students to use their hands and mime placing a hat on their heads.) When you've thought of everything you can for that side, take the hat off. Stop thinking like that person.

Step 4: Think like the other side. (Reveal the red hat but don't put it on yet.) You may have enjoyed thinking about the first side — but this one? Maybe not so much. But we have to pretend to love this side. We don't say "eww" or make faces. So you put on that hat and think their thoughts. (Introduce the gesture of picking up a hat, putting it on, thinking, taking it off, then switching to the other hat.)

Ask yourself: What is good about it? What would someone who loves this side say? Thinking like the other side is hard. Here are a couple writer tricks to help you.
• Close your eyes and picture a person — maybe someone you know — who would really love this choice. What do they like? Why would someone choose this? What would they say is good about it?
• Have you ever seen this topic/side in real life? A place, a person, a thing? What did you notice? That might help you think of more details that make someone like this.
• What have you heard about this topic/side? What have your friends, family, or teachers said about this?

Remember, you are only pretending to like this side. You're just borrowing that person's brain for a minute. Only after thinking through both sides carefully can a writer determine which one is stronger.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I think through both sides before I pick one.

Step 1: Name both sides. My topic is: What is the best treat — a candy bar or ice cream? (Display the candy bar & ice cream T-Chart.) Those are my two choices. I'm not picking yet. I'm just naming them.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. My first thought is already in my head — but I'm not saying it yet. (Place hand over mouth.) I have to think through both sides first.

Step 3: Think like one side. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I'm putting on my Candy Bar thinking cap. Candy bars are just… good. (Long pause.) Hmm. That's not a detail. I need to think smaller. What exactly happens when you eat a candy bar? (Close eyes.) I'm imagining a candy bar in my hands. I unwrap it. Ahh… I smell the chocolate. That's a detail! And then I take a bite. Oooh… and sometimes there's yummy things inside. Like caramel that is gooey and stretchy. Or peanut butter that's creamy. Or nuts make it crunchy. Those are all details for why someone would love a candy bar. I'm done thinking like a candy bar person. (Take the hat off.)

Step 4: Think like the other side. (Hold up the red hat but don't put it on yet.) Now I have to think like someone who loves ice cream. I mean it's fine — but I don't personally love it. I definitely need to borrow someone else's brain. (Put on the red hat.) Let me close my eyes and picture someone who really loves ice cream. (Close eyes.) I can picture someone standing at an ice cream counter, totally excited, trying to choose between all those flavors… stacking two scoops on a waffle cone… licking it before it melts… adding hot fudge and sprinkles on a big sundae…

I need to keep going. I could think about what I've seen at ice cream stores. Like I've seen friends mix two flavors together in a swirl. I've heard people say they love trying new flavors. Oh, milkshakes are made from ice cream. That's a good thing.

Today, we are learning how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic so that we can eventually figure out the strongest side.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example.
1. Name both sides. The topic is: Which is better — outdoor or indoor recess? (Display both sides. Point to each.) Two choices. We are not picking yet — just naming them.
2. Hand over mouth. You may already have a favorite but don't say it! (Hand over mouth.) We have to think through both sides first.
3. Think like one side. (Blue hat on — students mime.) With your Outdoor-Recess thinking cap on, what would someone who loves outdoor recess say? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard running, climbing, swings, slide, monkey bars, playing with a ball. But wait — what else can you say besides just the recess equipment? Think smaller. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard shouting and laughing, racing friends, playing with kids from other classes, having all that space to run. (Hat off — students mime.) See how thinking smaller gave us more details?
4. Think like the other side. Now we have to think like someone who loves indoor recess — even if that's not you. (Red hat on — students mime.) Close your eyes and picture someone who gets excited when it rains because that means recess is inside and what do you get to do? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard Legos, drawing, board games, puzzles, sitting wherever you want, playing house. Great thinking from both sides!

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic before picking one.

During Independent Writing Time, you and your partner will think through Which season is best — summer or winter. When I project a topic, put on your blue hat and together I want you & your partner to think every detail you can for that side. Then switch pretend hats and think like someone who loves the other side. See how many details you & your partner can come up with for each side. Let's go be writers!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (2 of 2) — Grade 2

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Yesterday we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic — putting on each thinking cap and pushing ourselves to think of small, specific details for both sides. Today I'm going to teach you how to jot down the details you think of for each side. This will bring us one step closer to determining the strongest side.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Yesterday we thought about both sides of a persuasive topic. But thinking alone isn't enough — if writers only think through details in their heads, those ideas slip away before they ever make it into writing. Jotting captures each detail on paper during prewriting. Jotting means writing something down quickly and simply — just enough to remember the thinking. We jot a couple words — and a quick picture if we need to. (Connect to research unit jotting if previously taught — SKILL 1, Days 2-3.) We used jotting before when we were doing research & collecting fact phrases from texts.

WHY the skill is important | If writers only think through details in their heads, ideas slip away. Jotting captures each detail on paper so it doesn't get lost.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Write one choice at the top of each side of the T-Chart. Write one choice next to the blue hat and one choice next to the red hat.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. Resist blurting out an opinion. We are going to THINK about both sides, one at a time.

Step 3: Think like one side & jot. (Reveal the blue hat.) Remember to put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best. (Students mime placing a hat on their heads.) As you think of a detail, jot it on its own line on that side of the T-Chart. Writers jot a couple words — just enough to remind them of the detail they thought of. Then, when you think of another detail for that same side, write it below the one before it, stacking down that same side. All of the details for that one choice are on the same side.

If you fill up all the lines on that side — don't stop and don't switch to the other side yet. Grab a second T-Chart and keep jotting on that same side. The other side stays empty for now — that's OK. You are still thinking like a blue hat person. Stay in that thinking cap until every detail is captured. (Remove blue hat. Students mime.)

Step 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Put on the red hat. Students mime.) Now think like someone who loves the OTHER choice. Use the same thinking strategies. Say each detail out loud. Then jot it on its own line on that side of the T-Chart.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I jot details for both sides of my persuasive topic.

Step 1: Name both sides. Yesterday my topic was: What is the best treat — a candy bar or ice cream? (Display a blank T-Chart.) The first thing I have to do is write one choice at the top of each side. (Write candy bar on the left & ice cream on the right.) There — both sides are named.

Step 2: Hand over mouth. I already know which one I love — (hand over mouth) — but I'm jotting both sides first because that's what persuasive writers do.

Step 3: Think like one side & jot. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I've got my Candy bar thinking cap on. Yesterday I thought of several details that are great about candy bars. I need to rethink them, one at a time, and jot them on the Candy bar side of the T-Chart.

Chocolate melts in your mouth — that's a detail. I need to jot that under Candy Bar. But I also want to be quick about it. I use shorthand and abbreviations — just enough so I remember the detail: "choc melt in mouth."

(Look up and think.) Caramel inside is gooey and stretchy. (Slide finger below the previous detail.) Next detail goes right below the first one — same side. (Jot "caramel = gooey, stretchy.")
• Repeat with "creamy PB" and "crunchy nuts."

(At some point demonstrate what to do when one side is full.) Wow — I filled up this whole side! But wait — I just thought of another one — chocolate is sweet. (Look at the full T-Chart.) There is no more space on this side. Do I stop? No! I grab a second T-Chart. (Display a second T-Chart.) I write Candy bar at the top of this same side. (Model how to jot "sweet.")

OK, I've thought of everything I can for this side. (Take the hat off.) I'm done thinking like a person who loves Candy bars.

Step 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Put on the red hat.) I put on the thinking cap of someone who loves ice cream. (Point at T-Chart and the right side.) Any details I come up with now, will all go on the right side — under "Ice cream."
• I'm picturing someone at the counter choosing a flavor. (Jot "many flavors.")
• I'm picturing someone who is licking his cone because it's starting to melt. (Jot "lick.")
• I'm picturing someone with different scoops. (Jot "stack scoops" and "try new flavors.")

Today, we are learning how to think & jot details for both sides of a persuasive topic. This is what writers do before determining the strongest side.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Yesterday, you thought about: What is better — outdoor or indoor recess? Help me jot down those details. (Reveal a new T-Chart.)

1. Name both sides. Where should I write "Outdoor?" Point in the air. Yes, right here next to the blue hat. And where do I write down the other choice — "Indoor?" Point in the air. Yep, right here by the red hat.

2. Hand over mouth.

3. Think like one side. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — toys, Lego towers, draw, board games, etc. (Model how to start a second T-Chart when one side gets full.)

4. Think like the other side. (Switch hats.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — swing on swings, go down slide, hang on monkey bars, play with friends in other classes, etc.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think & jot down details for BOTH sides of a persuasive. This is an important step before we can determine the strongest side.

During Independent Writing Time, you will fill out a T-Chart for Which season is best — Summer or Winter. This time you will work alone. (Yesterday you brainstormed with a partner. Today, you will jot down the details by yourself.) Think of all the details you can for one side before switching to the other side. And if you need a second T-Chart, I've got extra ones right here. Let's go be writers!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #3: Write an opinion — Grade 2

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Up until now, everything we have done in our persuasive unit has fallen under prewriting. We've listed details for both sides and figured out the strongest one. Now it's time to start drafting — and the very first thing a persuasive writer does is tell the audience his opinion. Today, I'm going to teach you how to write out the opinion at the beginning of any persuasive writing.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
All writing has a beginning, middle, and end — like a train with an engine, middle cars, and a caboose. That's a complete train and complete writing.

WHAT the skill is | In persuasive writing, the engine is the opinion sentence. This is where the writer tells the reader which side he chose and what he thinks.

WHY the skill is important | The reader needs to know right away that the writer is sharing an opinion. Starting with an opinion sentence tells the reader: this is what I think. Without an opinion sentence at the beginning of persuasive, the reader doesn't know what side the writer is on.

HOW the skill works |
STEP 1. Name the strongest side. Look back at your T-Chart. Find the side circled. Find the word(s) written next to the hat (on the strongest side). Use that word or those words in the first sentence.

STEP 2. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. (Connect to SKILL #1 — opinion signal words.) These words signal to the reader that an opinion is coming. Choose 3 to test out in Step 3.

STEP 3. Put the two parts together. Say it in one sentence out loud: strongest side + opinion words. Name the strongest side AND one of the opinion words/phrases in one sentence.
• Then, say the strongest side again with a different opinion word/phrase.
• Try out a couple different sentences by saying them out loud.
• You are sharing the same opinion each time; you're just saying it a little differently. So listen to the different ways you come up with. Pick the one that is easiest to say and easiest to understand.
• The one that sounds the best is the sentence to write/draw.

STEP 4. Write the sentence. After reading this first sentence, the audience will know exactly WHAT the writer thinks.

(NOTE: Stop there. The first sentence only names the opinion. No details. No "because.")

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I write my opinion sentence.

STEP 1. Name the strongest side. I look back at my T-Chart. (Point to the T-Chart.) I circled this side — Candy bar. That was my strongest side. It had the most details, the most proof. (Point to the word "Candy bar" next to the blue hat.) That's the word I need in my first sentence.

STEP 2. Choose 3 opinion words or phrases. Now I need to pick 3 opinion words/phrases to try out. (Point to the opinion word anchor chart.) I'm going to try these — My favorite…, best…, I like… (Write on the board.) I have a few choices. Let me try them out.

STEP 3. Put the two parts together. Now I put the two parts together — 1 of the opinion phrases plus "Candy bar," the strongest side. I'm going to try all three out loud and see which one sounds best.
• "best" + Candy bar. (Pause & think.) "The best treat is a candy bar." Pause. Hmm. That works. I like that, but let me try the next one to see if I like it any better.
• "My favorite…" + Candy bar. (Pause & think.) "My favorite treat is a candy bar." Ooh — I like that one too. I'll try one more way to say my opinion.
• "I like…" + Candy bar. (Pause & think.) "I like candy bars the best." Pause. That works too!

All three are opinion sentences. They all name my side. I think I like the second one. It sounds strong. It sounds like an opinion. And it tells my reader exactly which side I chose.

STEP 4. Write the sentence. So now I need to write my opinion. This will be my very first sentence on lined paper. (Write slowly while narrating: My… favorite… treat… is… a… candy… bar.) (Put the pencil/marker down.) And I stop. Right there. No because. No details. My reader knows what I think. The beginning is just my opinion.

Today, we are learning how to use our T-Chart and opinion words to write the beginning sentence of any persuasive writing.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example. (Reveal the T-Chart of best recess — outdoor or indoor.)

1. Name the strongest side. Which side did we determine was the strongest yesterday? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Yes — outdoor recess! How do you know? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Right, because it has the most details. So we want to use the words "outdoor recess" in our opinion sentence.

2. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. Look at the anchor chart. We also need to choose some opinion words from the chart. How about: "I think…, I believe…, The best…"

3. Put the two parts together. Now it's time to put those two parts together.
• "I think…" + outdoor recess. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard "I think outdoor recess is better than indoor recess."
• "I believe…" + outdoor recess. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard "I believe outdoor recess is the best kind of recess."
• "The best…" + outdoor recess. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard "The best recess is outdoor recess."

Which one sounds strongest? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I agree, "I think outdoor recess is better than indoor recess" is a clear, strong opinion. That's the first sentence to write in your persuasive.

Today, we are learning how to use opinion words and our strongest side from the T-Chart to write the first sentence of our persuasive piece.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
During Independent Writing Time, you will get out your T-Chart on what is the best season — Summer or Winter? I want you to follow the same process that I just taught you: 1. Name the strongest side. 2. Choose 3 opinion words. 3. Put the parts together. I want you to write 3 opinion sentences — each one using a different opinion word with the strongest side. Let's go be writers!
